sections.title: A white ball without a stem
sections.text: The fruiting body of Calvatia gigantea is a large, globose to irregular sphere, sometimes slightly flattened, usually white and smooth to gently bumpy. It is commonly 10–80 cm across and attaches to the ground by a subtle base or mycelial cord. It has no stem or differentiated cap, and no gills or tubes: nearly the whole interior is fertile tissue.

sections.title: A cross-section reveals maturity
sections.text: In a longitudinal cut, the young gleba is compact, firm and uniformly white. As it matures, it turns yellowish green, then olive to brown and powdery as spores form. The outer skin, white at first, may crack or break away at maturity, releasing the spore dust.

sections.title: Habitat and season
sections.text: This saprotrophic species grows on the ground, often in meadows, pastures, lawns, field edges and clearings, singly or in small groups. It fruits mainly from late summer through autumn, depending on local climate.

sections.title: Identification and caution
sections.text: Exceptional size, a globose shape and a uniformly plain interior characterize mature specimens. A top-to-bottom cut should show white flesh with no developing cap, stem or gills: young eggs of poisonous Amanita species can look like a white ball from the outside. Never eat a specimen without certain expert identification.

traits: Globose to irregular white fruiting body, usually 10–80 cm across, with no stem or differentiated cap
Cross-section firm, compact and uniformly white when young; gleba turns yellowish green, then olive-brown and powdery at maturity
No gills or tubes: fertile tissue occupies nearly the entire interior
Grows on soil in meadows, pastures, lawns, field edges or clearings, singly or in small groups
Fruits mainly from late summer through autumn; white outer skin may crack at maturity
safetyNote: Reported edibility applies only to young, fresh specimens that are uniformly white inside. A full longitudinal cut must rule out any cap, stem or gills, since a poisonous Amanita egg can resemble a white ball. An illustration cannot validate a foraged specimen: eat only after certain expert identification.
